after: ## Movement along a curve or a shift?
alt: Left: when the product’s own price falls from P1 to P2, quantity demanded extends from Q1 to Q2 along the same demand curve. Right: when another factor changes, such as a rival’s price rising, the whole demand curve shifts right from D to D1.
caption: Own price moves you along the curve; anything else shifts it.

after: ## Shifts in practice: telling the story of a market
alt: Demand shifts right for loose coffee when pod prices rise, for pods when machine prices fall, for mobility aids as the population ages, and with the seasons; it shifts left for products bought by young adults. Supply shifts left with an indirect tax or higher costs and right with a subsidy or new technology.
caption: Explain the mechanism behind each shift, not just its direction.

after: ## Shifts in practice: telling the story of a market
alt: Demand shifts right from D to D1 and supply shifts right from S to S1. Quantity rises from Q1 to Q2, but the effect on price depends on the relative size of the two shifts; with equal shifts, as drawn, price is unchanged.
caption: With two shifts, one variable is certain and the other depends on their sizes.

alt: Demand Qd = 900 − 30P and supply Qs = 100 + 50P meet at $10 and 600 cartons. A $1.60 tax shifts supply left to Qs = 20 + 50P, giving a new equilibrium at $11 and 570 cartons. The price rises by only $1.00, so each firm keeps $9.40 a carton instead of $10.
caption: Customers pay $1.00 of the $1.60 tax; firms absorb the rest and sell less.

after: ## Drawing a demand and supply diagram
alt: A labelled diagram with demand shifting right from D to D1. Numbered points show the five elements: labelled axes, labelled D and S curves, the original equilibrium with dotted lines to P1 and Q1, the shifted curve with a direction arrow, and the new equilibrium at P2 and Q2.
caption: Five labels turn a sketch into a constructed diagram.

after: ## Price elasticity of demand: beyond the formula
alt: A PED scale from 0 to above 1. A price rise raises revenue when demand is perfectly inelastic or inelastic, leaves it unchanged at 1 and reduces it when demand is elastic. Demand is more elastic with close substitutes, non-necessities, a large share of income, little loyalty and more time. Pricing decisions are about profit, not just revenue.
caption: PED predicts what a price change does to revenue; profit also depends on costs.

after: ## Worked example 2: choosing between price rises
alt: Brockley Gyms earns $400,000 a month from 10,000 members at $40. A 10% rise to $44 gives $422,400 (up $22,400) if PED is −0.4 and members fall to 9,600, but $360,800 (down $39,200) if PED is −1.8 and members fall to 8,200. Long contracts and few rivals point to −0.4; nearby budget gyms point to −1.8.
caption: The same price rise gains or loses revenue depending on the PED estimate.

alt: A YED scale: below 0 inferior, 0 to +1 normal and income inelastic, above +1 normal and income elastic. Brockley’s off-peak budget membership falls 2% when incomes rise 5% (YED −0.4, inferior); its premium personal training rises 9% (YED +1.8, income elastic).
caption: Positive YED means a normal good, negative an inferior one; the size shows how strongly demand follows income.
